1	Web corpora increasingly contain machine-generated text.
2	Recent estimates place the synthetic fraction at 20--60\% of crawled data~\citep{cheng2025contamination}, and this share grows as language models are deployed for content production at scale.
3	Training on such contaminated data has concrete consequences: \citet{shumailov2024model} show that recursive training on model outputs leads to irreversible quality degradation---\emph{model collapse}---and \citet{dohmatob2025strong} prove under scaling-law regimes that even a vanishingly small synthetic fraction suffices to trigger this failure mode, ruling out data scaling as a remedy.
4	A central difficulty is that the contamination proportion in any given corpus is unknown: synthetic text enters through diverse, uncoordinated channels with no centralized provenance record.
5	The prevalence, severity, and opacity of synthetic contamination make contamination-aware pretraining a practical necessity.
6	
7	A natural response is \emph{detect-and-reweight}: train a classifier to estimate each sample's synthetic probability $q(x)$, then suppress likely-synthetic samples via the weighting function $w(x) = (1 - q(x))^b$.
8	\citet{drayson2025detection} demonstrate this approach for model collapse prevention and show that the exponent $b$ critically determines outcomes---their optimal values range from $b{=}10$ for models at ${\leq}360$M parameters to $b{=}1$ at 1.7B, and misspecification degrades results substantially.
9	Selecting $b$ therefore requires per-model validation-set grid search, with computational cost scaling linearly in the number of candidates (six training runs in a typical sweep).
10	Other approaches assume even stronger supervision: \citet{he2025golden} derive theoretically optimal weights from convergence analysis but require the exact contamination ratio $\rho$, which is precisely what is unavailable in practice.
11	Hard detection-and-removal strategies~\citep{feng2025beyond} discard borderline samples entirely, sacrificing the smooth reweighting that continuous $q$-scores enable.
12	
13	Given per-sample detector scores $q(x)$, how should one choose $b$ without a validation set or known contamination proportion?
14	We formulate this as a dual-constrained optimization over each training batch: find the smallest $b$ that ensures the weighted effective real proportion $\aeff(b)$ reaches a quality threshold $\tau$, while keeping Kish's effective sample size $\mathrm{ESS}(b)$ above a stability floor $\nmin$.
15	The quality constraint has theoretical grounding: convergence rate under contaminated training improves with the effective real-data fraction~\citep{wang2026survive}, motivating a lower bound on $\aeff$.
16	The stability constraint prevents extreme weight concentration that degrades gradient quality.
17	These two requirements exhibit a natural opposition.
18	$\aeff(b)$ increases monotonically in $b$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:monotone}), yielding a lower bound $\btau$---the minimum exponent needed to achieve the target quality.
19	$\mathrm{ESS}(b)$ decreases monotonically, yielding an upper bound $\bess$---the maximum exponent before gradient stability degrades.
20	The adaptive exponent $\bstar = \btau$ when the feasible region $[\btau, \bess]$ is non-empty, embodying a \emph{minimum intervention principle}: apply the least downweighting sufficient to meet the quality target, preserving as much effective training data as possible.
21	When the constraints conflict ($\btau > \bess$), the stability ceiling takes precedence.
22	
23	This minimum-intervention semantics distinguishes the method from the alternative of maximizing $b$ subject only to ESS stability.
24	Among batches that require reweighting, the dual-constraint solver selects $\bstar$ via the $\aeff$ bound in 40\% of cases, with mean $\bstar{=}1.67$; the ESS-only variant would choose $b{=}4.15$ in these same batches, 2.5$\times$ more aggressive.
25	The remaining 49.9\% of batches have sufficient real-data content to skip reweighting entirely ($\bstar{=}0$).
26	The per-batch $\bstar$ distribution (median 0.87, mean 1.40) adapts continuously to each batch's contamination composition without any held-out signal.
27	
28	On Qwen3-0.6B continued pretraining with 40\% synthetic contamination (132M+ tokens from FineWeb), adaptive reweighting achieves comparable performance to the grid-searched optimum: PPL 17.653 vs.\ grid-best $b{=}0.3$ at 17.640 (gap 0.013, comparable to cross-seed standard deviation ${\sim}0.007$), capturing ${\sim}76\%$ of the grid-best improvement over uniform (\S\ref{sec:results}).
29	The grid sweep requires multiple complete training runs to identify this optimum; the adaptive method requires one.
30	The ESS-only variant (maximum intervention) yields mean PPL 17.723---no better than the uniform baseline (17.694)---confirming that maximum intervention provides no improvement while minimum intervention does.
31	A lightweight TF-IDF + Logistic Regression detector (AUC\,=\,0.939, calibrated ECE\,=\,0.048) suffices throughout, suggesting that score calibration may matter as much as raw classification accuracy for provenance-based reweighting---though confirming this requires controlled comparison across multiple detectors.
32	
33	Our contributions:
34	\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
35	\item A dual-constrained framework for adaptive exponent selection: $\bstar = \inf\{b \geq 0 : \aeff(b) \geq \tau\}$ subject to $\mathrm{ESS}(b) \geq \nmin$, computed per-batch from detector scores with minimum-intervention semantics (\S\ref{sec:method}).
36	\item Empirical evidence that adaptive $\bstar$ achieves comparable performance to grid-searched best at zero validation cost, and that minimum intervention (dual constraint) outperforms maximum intervention (ESS-only) across three seeds (\S\ref{sec:results}).
37	\item A demonstration that a lightweight TF-IDF + LR detector with calibrated $q$-scores supports effective reweighting, achieving results comparable to stronger neural detectors (\S\ref{sec:experiments}).
38	\end{itemize}
39

file.content:
Web corpora increasingly contain machine-generated text.
Recent estimates place the synthetic fraction at 20--60\% of crawled data~\citep{cheng2025contamination}, and this share grows as language models are deployed for content production at scale.
Training on such contaminated data has concrete consequences: \citet{shumailov2024model} show that recursive training on model outputs leads to irreversible quality degradation---\emph{model collapse}---and \citet{dohmatob2025strong} prove under scaling-law regimes that even a vanishingly small synthetic fraction suffices to trigger this failure mode, ruling out data scaling as a remedy.
A central difficulty is that the contamination proportion in any given corpus is unknown: synthetic text enters through diverse, uncoordinated channels with no centralized provenance record.
The prevalence, severity, and opacity of synthetic contamination make contamination-aware pretraining a practical necessity.

A natural response is \emph{detect-and-reweight}: train a classifier to estimate each sample's synthetic probability $q(x)$, then suppress likely-synthetic samples via the weighting function $w(x) = (1 - q(x))^b$.
\citet{drayson2025detection} demonstrate this approach for model collapse prevention and show that the exponent $b$ critically determines outcomes---their optimal values range from $b{=}10$ for models at ${\leq}360$M parameters to $b{=}1$ at 1.7B, and misspecification degrades results substantially.
Selecting $b$ therefore requires per-model validation-set grid search, with computational cost scaling linearly in the number of candidates (six training runs in a typical sweep).
Other approaches assume even stronger supervision: \citet{he2025golden} derive theoretically optimal weights from convergence analysis but require the exact contamination ratio $\rho$, which is precisely what is unavailable in practice.
Hard detection-and-removal strategies~\citep{feng2025beyond} discard borderline samples entirely, sacrificing the smooth reweighting that continuous $q$-scores enable.

Given per-sample detector scores $q(x)$, how should one choose $b$ without a validation set or known contamination proportion?
We formulate this as a dual-constrained optimization over each training batch: find the smallest $b$ that ensures the weighted effective real proportion $\aeff(b)$ reaches a quality threshold $\tau$, while keeping Kish's effective sample size $\mathrm{ESS}(b)$ above a stability floor $\nmin$.
The quality constraint has theoretical grounding: convergence rate under contaminated training improves with the effective real-data fraction~\citep{wang2026survive}, motivating a lower bound on $\aeff$.
The stability constraint prevents extreme weight concentration that degrades gradient quality.
These two requirements exhibit a natural opposition.
$\aeff(b)$ increases monotonically in $b$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:monotone}), yielding a lower bound $\btau$---the minimum exponent needed to achieve the target quality.
$\mathrm{ESS}(b)$ decreases monotonically, yielding an upper bound $\bess$---the maximum exponent before gradient stability degrades.
The adaptive exponent $\bstar = \btau$ when the feasible region $[\btau, \bess]$ is non-empty, embodying a \emph{minimum intervention principle}: apply the least downweighting sufficient to meet the quality target, preserving as much effective training data as possible.
When the constraints conflict ($\btau > \bess$), the stability ceiling takes precedence.

This minimum-intervention semantics distinguishes the method from the alternative of maximizing $b$ subject only to ESS stability.
Among batches that require reweighting, the dual-constraint solver selects $\bstar$ via the $\aeff$ bound in 40\% of cases, with mean $\bstar{=}1.67$; the ESS-only variant would choose $b{=}4.15$ in these same batches, 2.5$\times$ more aggressive.
The remaining 49.9\% of batches have sufficient real-data content to skip reweighting entirely ($\bstar{=}0$).
The per-batch $\bstar$ distribution (median 0.87, mean 1.40) adapts continuously to each batch's contamination composition without any held-out signal.

On Qwen3-0.6B continued pretraining with 40\% synthetic contamination (132M+ tokens from FineWeb), adaptive reweighting achieves comparable performance to the grid-searched optimum: PPL 17.653 vs.\ grid-best $b{=}0.3$ at 17.640 (gap 0.013, comparable to cross-seed standard deviation ${\sim}0.007$), capturing ${\sim}76\%$ of the grid-best improvement over uniform (\S\ref{sec:results}).
The grid sweep requires multiple complete training runs to identify this optimum; the adaptive method requires one.
The ESS-only variant (maximum intervention) yields mean PPL 17.723---no better than the uniform baseline (17.694)---confirming that maximum intervention provides no improvement while minimum intervention does.
A lightweight TF-IDF + Logistic Regression detector (AUC\,=\,0.939, calibrated ECE\,=\,0.048) suffices throughout, suggesting that score calibration may matter as much as raw classification accuracy for provenance-based reweighting---though confirming this requires controlled comparison across multiple detectors.

Our contributions:
\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
\item A dual-constrained framework for adaptive exponent selection: $\bstar = \inf\{b \geq 0 : \aeff(b) \geq \tau\}$ subject to $\mathrm{ESS}(b) \geq \nmin$, computed per-batch from detector scores with minimum-intervention semantics (\S\ref{sec:method}).
\item Empirical evidence that adaptive $\bstar$ achieves comparable performance to grid-searched best at zero validation cost, and that minimum intervention (dual constraint) outperforms maximum intervention (ESS-only) across three seeds (\S\ref{sec:results}).
\item A demonstration that a lightweight TF-IDF + LR detector with calibrated $q$-scores supports effective reweighting, achieving results comparable to stronger neural detectors (\S\ref{sec:experiments}).
\end{itemize}

file.content:
\subsection{Main Comparison}

Table~\ref{tab:main} reports held-out perplexity across methods and seeds.
Adaptive reweighting achieves comparable performance to grid-best: PPL 17.653 vs.\ grid-best $b{=}0.3$ at 17.640 (seed 42), a gap of 0.013 that falls within the range of cross-seed standard deviation (${\sim}0.007$).
This comes at zero validation cost---grid search requires $|\mathcal{B}|$ complete training runs (seven in our sweep), whereas adaptive requires one.

The grid-$b$ sweep reveals monotonically increasing PPL from $b{=}0.3$ to $b{=}5.0$ (17.640 to 17.818 on seed 42), confirming that exponent selection is consequential.
The optimal $b{=}0.3$ differs from the $b{=}10$ reported by \citet{drayson2025detection} at comparable model scale, underscoring the model-dependence of fixed-exponent selection.

ESS-only (maximum intervention) yields mean PPL $17.723 {\pm} 0.006$ across three seeds, providing no improvement over uniform ($17.694 {\pm} 0.008$).
Removing $\aeff$ and maximizing $b$ subject only to $\mathrm{ESS} \geq \nmin$ over-downweights borderline samples, providing direct evidence for the minimum-intervention principle.

The Golden Ratio oracle~\citep{he2025golden} achieves PPL 17.654 (seed 42) using known provenance labels.
Adaptive reaches 17.653 on the same seed without provenance access, suggesting the dual constraint recovers near-optimal weights from noisy detector scores alone.

The adaptive $\bstar$ distribution (median 0.87, IQR $[0.54, 1.51]$, mean 1.40) confirms that most batches need only moderate intervention.
Among the 50.1\% of batches requiring reweighting, $\aeff$ is the binding constraint in 40.1\% of cases (mean $\bstar{=}1.67$); the ESS-only variant would select $b{=}4.15$ in these same batches---$2.5{\times}$ more aggressive.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lcccc@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Method} & \textbf{Seed 42} & \textbf{Seed 123} & \textbf{Seed 456} & \textbf{Mean} \\
\midrule
Uniform               & 17.694 & 17.686 & 17.702 & 17.694 \\
Grid-best ($b{=}0.3$)$^\dagger$ & \textbf{17.640} & --     & --     & --     \\
Grid ($b{=}0.5$)       & 17.651 & \textbf{17.638} & \textbf{17.650} & \textbf{17.646} \\
ESS-only               & 17.730 & 17.720 & 17.719 & 17.723 \\
Golden Ratio$^\ddagger$ & 17.654 & --     & --     & --     \\
\midrule
Adaptive (ours)        & 17.653 & 17.643 & 17.657 & 17.651 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Held-out perplexity (PPL, $\downarrow$) at $\rho{=}0.4$.
Grid-best selects the optimal fixed $b$ post-hoc from seven candidates.
$^\dagger$Seed 42 only; cross-seed pending.
$^\ddagger$Requires known provenance labels (oracle); seed 42 only.
Best per column in \textbf{bold}.}
\label{tab:main}
\end{table}

\subsection{Sensitivity Analysis}

\paragraph{Quality threshold $\tau$.}
Table~\ref{tab:tau} varies $\tau$ while holding $n_{\min} = 2$ (seed 42).
All values in $\tau \in [0.5, 0.8]$ improve over uniform, with $\tau = 0.8$ achieving the lowest PPL (17.653).
Higher $\tau$ demands greater $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}$, forcing the solver to increase $b^*$: mean $\bar{b}^*$ rises monotonically from 0.39 at $\tau{=}0.5$ to 3.08 at $\tau{=}0.95$.
Below 0.8, reweighting is too gentle to fully exploit the detector signal; above, $b^*$ inflates past diminishing returns and PPL degrades.
The range $[0.5, 0.8]$ provides a wide safe operating region, with $\tau = 0.8$ as the recommended default.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}cccc@{}}
\toprule
$\tau$ & \textbf{PPL} & $\Delta_{\mathrm{unif}}$ & $\bar{b}^*$ \\
\midrule
0.50 & 17.688 & $-$0.006 & 0.39 \\
0.60 & 17.681 & $-$0.013 & 0.59 \\
0.70 & 17.679 & $-$0.015 & 0.89 \\
\textbf{0.80} & \textbf{17.653} & $\mathbf{-0.041}$ & \textbf{1.40} \\
0.90 & 17.712 & $+$0.018 & 2.36 \\
0.95 & 17.723 & $+$0.029 & 3.08 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Sensitivity to $\tau$ (seed 42, $n_{\min}{=}2$, $\rho{=}0.4$).
$\Delta_{\mathrm{unif}}$: PPL change vs.\ uniform baseline (17.694).
$\bar{b}^*$: mean adaptive exponent across batches.}
\label{tab:tau}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Minimum ESS $n_{\min}$.}
Removing the ESS floor ($n_{\min} = 1$) allows $b^*$ to inflate to mean 7.20, degrading PPL to 17.789---0.095 worse than uniform.
At $n_{\min} = 2$ ($= \lfloor B/2 \rfloor$ for batch size $B{=}4$), PPL stabilizes at 17.653; $n_{\min} = 3$ yields a comparable 17.644.
The coupling $n_{\min} = \lfloor B/2 \rfloor$ provides a configuration-aware default that balances reweighting headroom against gradient stability.
Setting $n_{\min} = 4$ ($= B$) forces $\bstar = 0$ for all batches, recovering uniform training (PPL 17.695).

\subsection{Higher Contamination ($\rho = 0.6$)}

To test robustness to contamination level, we evaluate at $\rho = 0.6$ (seed 42).
Adaptive $\bstar$ achieves PPL 17.740, improving over uniform (17.766) by 0.026.
ESS-only yields 17.770, providing no improvement over uniform (gap 0.004)---at higher contamination, maximum intervention retreats to uniform-level performance.
Grid $b{=}0.5$ achieves 17.704, outperforming adaptive by 0.036; the larger gap relative to $\rho{=}0.4$ suggests that the default $\tau{=}0.8$ may benefit from adjustment at higher contamination rates.
Cross-seed verification at $\rho = 0.6$ is ongoing.

We introduced Minimum Intervention Reweighting, a dual-constraint framework for contamination-aware pretraining that derives per-batch exponents $\bstar$ without validation data.
The method finds the smallest $b$ satisfying $\aeff(b) \geq \tau$ subject to $\mathrm{ESS}(b) \geq \nmin$, enforcing a minimum intervention principle: apply only as much downweighting as needed to meet a quality floor, no more.

At 0.6B scale with 40\% synthetic contamination, adaptive $\bstar$ achieves comparable performance to grid-search-optimal $b{=}0.3$ (PPL 17.653 vs.\ 17.640; gap 0.013, within range of cross-seed variance ${\sim}0.007$), capturing ${\sim}76\%$ of the grid-best improvement over uniform (17.694) while eliminating the grid search entirely.
ESS-only maximum intervention (PPL $17.723 {\pm} 0.006$) provides no improvement over uniform, confirming that minimum intervention is the better operating point; at $\rho = 0.6$, ESS-only retreats to uniform-level performance while adaptive $\bstar$ still improves.
The quality threshold $\tau$ is robust across $[0.5, 0.8]$---all values in this range improve over uniform---and a lightweight TF-IDF + logistic regression detector (AUC\,=\,0.939) suffices when calibrated (ECE\,=\,0.048).

Our evaluation is limited to a single model scale (0.6B) and controlled injection setting.
Whether the calibration-over-discrimination observation generalizes remains a hypothesis pending multi-detector comparison.

Three directions merit investigation: (1)~scaling to larger models (3B+) to test whether $\tau$ and $\nmin$ defaults transfer across scales; (2)~controlled comparison across multiple detector families to verify the calibration hypothesis; (3)~evaluation on naturally contaminated web corpora where ground-truth provenance labels are unavailable.

Detect-and-reweight methods suppress likely-synthetic samples via $w(x) = (1-q(x))^b$, but the exponent $b$ critically determines outcomes and requires per-model grid search---typically multiple complete training runs---to tune.

The ESS-only variant (maximum intervention) provides no improvement over uniform training (PPL 17.723 vs.\ 17.694).
The quality threshold $\tau$ is robust across $[0.5, 0.8]$, and a lightweight TF-IDF + logistic regression detector (AUC = 0.939, calibrated ECE = 0.048) suffices, suggesting that score calibration may matter as much as raw classification accuracy.

Principled per-batch exponent derivation eliminates grid search while retaining the effectiveness of detect-and-reweight pretraining.
